_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 590 words, six questions in text order: detail/opinion, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase, and a final question that links the ending back to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Losing for a reason
subtitle: Fifteen-year-old Felix Amadi would rather lose an exciting game of chess than win a dull one. Rachel Dunn watched him play.

cards.text: Felix Amadi is fifteen and one of the strongest young chess players in the east of England, but if you ask him about his best game, he will show you one he lost. He sets up the pieces on the kitchen table, moving quickly, as if he has done this many times before. 'This is the one,' he says. 'I sacrificed my queen on move eleven. Completely unnecessary. My coach nearly fainted.' He lost forty moves later, to a player ranked far above him. 'It was the most fun I've ever had,' he says, and he clearly means it.
cards.question: Why does Felix consider this game to be his best?
choices: He beat a player ranked much higher than him.
He enjoyed it more than any other game.
His coach praised his decision to sacrifice his queen.
It was the shortest game he has ever played.
cards.highlight: It was the most fun I've ever had
cards.why: He lost the game, so A is wrong. What makes it his best is that 'it was the most fun I've ever had'. His coach 'nearly fainted', which is shock, not praise (C).

cards.text: This attitude has not always made him popular. His coach, a former county champion called Diane Rook, describes their early lessons as 'a battle of wills'. She wanted him to play safely, protect his pieces and wait for his opponents to make mistakes. Felix found this so boring that he once fell asleep during a tournament, while it was his turn to move. 'He woke up, looked at the board for two seconds and played the worst move I have ever seen,' Diane says. 'Then he smiled at me across the hall. I could have thrown the clock at him.'
cards.question: What can we infer about Diane's feelings at that tournament?
choices: She was proud that Felix stayed so calm.
She thought Felix was too tired to continue.
She found Felix's behaviour extremely frustrating.
She was amused by the move he played.
cards.highlight: I could have thrown the clock at him.
cards.why: 'I could have thrown the clock at him' shows she was furious. She may laugh about it now, but at the time she was not amused (D), and she never says he was too tired to go on (B).

cards.text: Things changed when Diane stopped trying to change him. Instead of telling him to avoid risks, she began asking him to explain them. Before any wild move, Felix now has to write down, in one sentence, what he hopes will happen. Often it does not, but the habit has made him think more carefully. 'It's not about winning less,' Diane says. 'It's about losing for a reason.' His rating has risen steadily ever since, which Felix finds slightly annoying. 'People keep expecting me to win now,' he complains. 'It ruins the surprise.'
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'Often it does not'?
choices: the habit of writing a sentence
what Felix hopes will happen
his chess rating
the risk Diane asks about
cards.why: 'It does not' means 'it does not happen', so 'it' is what Felix 'hopes will happen' after a wild move. The habit actually works, making him 'think more carefully', so A is wrong.

cards.text: At school, very few of his friends know how good he is. Felix prefers it that way. He plays football badly, he says, and enthusiastically, and he likes being 'just average at something'. His younger sister, Grace, is less impressed by his chess than by the fact that he can juggle four oranges. Last term his maths teacher discovered his rating online and announced it to the class. 'Everyone looked at me as if I'd grown another head,' Felix says. 'Then someone asked if I could do their homework, and it all went back to normal.'
cards.question: Why does the writer mention Felix's football?
choices: to suggest that he may give up chess for sport
to explain why his friends do not respect him
to compare his chess with his sister's hobbies
to show that he enjoys things he is not especially good at
cards.highlight: he likes being 'just average at something'
cards.why: He plays football 'badly… and enthusiastically' and likes being 'just average at something'. Nothing suggests he will give up chess (A), and his friends treat him normally rather than without respect (B).

cards.text: Of course, there is a serious side. Next spring Felix will play in the national under-sixteen championship, and he admits he is nervous. Diane would like him to 'play it straight' for once, with no sacrifices and no surprises, and he has promised to try. Whether he will keep that promise is another matter. When I ask him what he will do if he finds a crazy idea in the middle of an important game, he thinks for a moment. 'I'll write my sentence,' he says. 'And if the sentence is good enough, I'll play it.' Diane, listening from the doorway, closes her eyes.
cards.question: What does Diane mean when she asks Felix to 'play it straight'?
choices: play in a careful, sensible way
play more quickly than usual
play honestly, without cheating
play without help from his coach
cards.highlight: with no sacrifices and no surprises
cards.why: The phrase is explained straight after it: 'with no sacrifices and no surprises', in other words safe, sensible chess. Nothing suggests Felix has ever cheated, so C misreads 'straight'.

cards.text: Before I go, Felix sets up the board one more time. He wants to show me the game again, the one he lost, because he thinks he has found a better move eleven. Not a safer one, he points out: a better sacrifice. He has been working on it for two years. 'If I'd found this at the time,' he says, 'I think I might even have won.' He pauses, thinking about this possibility, and looks slightly disappointed. Then he resets the pieces and starts again from the beginning, as happy as anyone I have met all year.
cards.question: What does the ending suggest about Felix?
choices: He deeply regrets losing the game he showed the writer at the start.
He cares more about the ideas in a game than about the result.
He has finally decided to follow Diane's advice.
He is getting bored of studying the same game.
cards.why: The lost game from the opening returns, and the idea of winning it leaves him 'slightly disappointed', because the idea matters more to him than the result. He wants 'a better sacrifice', not a safer move, so C is wrong.
